background.title: Coordinates and reading a graph
background.html:
A graph has two number lines: the x-axis going across and the y-axis going up. They cross at the point (0, 0). A point is written (x, y): first go across, then up. (3, 7) is 3 right and 7 up; (−2, 4) is 2 left and 4 up.

For a function, the y-value is the output. The point (a, b) is on the graph of y = f(x) exactly when f(a) = b. So when the page says read the domain off the x-axis, it means: which x-values does the graph use? Read the range off the y-axis means: which y-values (heights) does the graph reach?

When a question says write down the coordinates of a point on a graph, you read them off the graph or the given information, with little or no working.

background.title: Straight lines: y = mx + c
background.html:
Every straight line that is not vertical has an equation y = mx + c.

  • m is the gradient: how much y changes when x goes up by 1. Through two points, m = (y2 − y1) ÷ (x2 − x1).
  • c is where the line crosses the y-axis, at the point (0, c).

Example: through (0, −4) and (3, 8), m = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and c = −4, so y = 4x − 4. A negative m means the line goes down from left to right. A horizontal line has the equation y = b and a vertical line x = a. A function whose graph is a straight line is called linear.

background.title: Putting numbers into a formula
background.html:
For f(x) = x2 + 1, f(3) means: put 3 in place of x. So f(3) = 32 + 1 = 10.

Put negative numbers in brackets: f(−2) = (−2)2 + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5, because a negative times a negative is positive. Careful: −x2 at x = 3 means −(32) = −9, not 9. The square is done before the minus.

Order of work: brackets first, then powers, then × and ÷, then + and −. So 2 × 4 − 16 + 1 = 8 − 16 + 1 = −7.

background.title: Solving and rearranging equations
background.html:
An equation stays true if you do the same thing to both sides. To solve it, undo what was done to x, in reverse order:

2x + 3 = 10 → subtract 3 from both sides: 2x = 7 → divide both sides by 2: x = 3.5.

Rearranging works the same way when there are only letters. To get y on its own in x = (2y + 5) ÷ 3:

  • multiply both sides by 3: 3x = 2y + 5;
  • subtract 5: 3x − 5 = 2y;
  • divide by 2: y = (3x − 5) ÷ 2.

This is exactly how you will find an inverse function today.

background.title: Inequalities and the number line
background.html:
• < less than, ≤ less than or equal to
  • > greater than, ≥ greater than or equal to
  • ≠ not equal to

x ≥ −3 means every number from −3 upwards, including −3 itself. 2 < x < 5 means every number between 2 and 5, but not 2 or 5.

Solve an inequality like an equation, with one extra rule: when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, flip the sign. 2 − x ≥ 0 → −x ≥ −2 → divide by −1 and flip: x ≤ 2.

On a number line or graph, a solid dot means the end is included (≤, ≥) and an open dot means it is not (<, >).

background.title: Square roots and dividing by zero
background.html:
√9 = 3, because 3 × 3 = 9. The √ sign always means the positive root (or 0), so a square root is never negative. But the equation x2 = 9 has two answers, 3 and −3, written x = ±3.

A negative number has no square root on the number line: √(−1) does not exist, because any number times itself is 0 or positive.

The reciprocal of a number is 1 divided by it: the reciprocal of 4 is 1/4. You cannot divide by zero, so 1/0 does not exist.

These two facts (no square root of a negative, no dividing by zero) decide almost every domain on this page.

background.title: Expanding brackets and factorising quadratics
background.html:
Expanding: multiply every part of one bracket by every part of the other. (x − 3)(x + 1) = x2 + x − 3x − 3 = x2 − 2x − 3.

Factorising goes backwards. For x2 − 2x − 3, find two numbers that multiply to −3 and add to −2: they are −3 and 1. So x2 − 2x − 3 = (x − 3)(x + 1).

To solve (x − 3)(x + 1) = 0: if two numbers multiply to 0, one of them must be 0, so x = 3 or x = −1.

Squaring a bracket: (x − 1)2 = (x − 1)(x − 1) = x2 − 2x + 1, not x2 + 1.

The Khan Academy page uses American words: factor means factorise, and a binomial is a bracket with two parts, like (x + 1).

terms.def: A rule that gives every allowed input exactly one output. f(x) = 2x + 3 is a function: it sends 4 to 11.
All the inputs (x-values) a function is allowed to take. For √x the domain is x ≥ 0.
All the outputs (y-values, f(x)) a function actually gives. For √x the range is f(x) ≥ 0. Always write it with f(x) or y, not x.
The function that undoes f, written f<sup>−1</sup>. If f sends 2 to 7, then f<sup>−1</sup> sends 7 back to 2. The −1 here is a label, not a power.
A function where every output comes from only one input. f(x) = 2x is one-to-one; f(x) = x<sup>2</sup> is not, because f(−2) = f(2) = 4.
Two functions done one after the other: the output of the first is the input of the second. (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)): do g first, then f.
A function made of different rules on different parts of its domain, for example f(x) = x + 1 for x < 0 and f(x) = 1 − x for x ≥ 0. Its graph is made of pieces.
Flip a picture over a line, like a mirror. Reflecting in the line y = x swaps the two coordinates: (3, 7) becomes (7, 3).
The pair of numbers (x, y) that says where a point is: x steps across, then y steps up, starting from (0, 0). The y-coordinate of (1, −4) is −4.
The two number lines of a graph: the x-axis going across and the y-axis going up. One is called an axis. They cross at (0, 0).
Where a graph meets an axis. The y-intercept: put x = 0. The x-intercepts: where y = 0. Give them as points, like (0, 3).
The zeros of a function are the x-values where its output is 0: solve f(x) = 0. Those solutions are also called the roots of the equation. On the graph, that is where it meets the x-axis.
How steep a line is: how much y goes up when x goes up by 1. Gradient = (change in y) ÷ (change in x). A negative gradient means the line goes down.
A linear function has the form f(x) = mx + c, so its graph is a straight line. Example: f(x) = 4x − 4.

A function or equation where the highest power of x is x<sup>2</sup>. It is written ax<sup>2</sup> + bx + c: a is the number in front of x<sup>2</sup>, b the number in front of x, c the number on its own. Its graph is a parabola.
The U-shaped curve you get from a quadratic ax<sup>2</sup> + bx + c. It opens upwards (U) when a, the number in front of x<sup>2</sup>, is positive and downwards (∩) when a is negative.
The turning point of a parabola: its lowest point (a minimum) if it opens upwards, its highest point (a maximum) if it opens downwards.
A point where a graph stops going up and starts going down (a maximum point), or the other way round (a minimum point).

A line that cuts a graph into two mirror-image halves. For a parabola y = ax<sup>2</sup> + bx + c it is the vertical line through the vertex, x = −b ÷ (2a). Example: y = x<sup>2</sup> − 2x − 3 gives x = 1.
A graph is symmetric about a line if folding along that line makes the two halves land exactly on each other.

A straight line that a graph gets closer and closer to, without reaching it, as the graph heads far out (x or y very large, positive or negative). It is drawn dashed and labelled with its equation, such as x = 2 or y = 1.
The bottom part of a fraction. In 3/(x − 2) the denominator is x − 2. It may never be 0.
A point where two graphs meet or cross. There both graphs have the same x and the same y.
A piece of maths made of numbers, letters and operations, with no = sign. Examples: 2 − x and x<sup>2</sup> + 1.
The small raised number, also called an exponent: x<sup>3</sup> = x × x × x. Negative and fraction powers exist too: x<sup>−1</sup> = 1/x and x<sup>1/2</sup> = √x, so x<sup>−1/2</sup> = 1/√x.
One divided by a number: the reciprocal of 4 is 1/4, and of f(x) is 1/f(x). The inverse f<sup>−1</sup>(x) is NOT the reciprocal.
Something you do to a number: add, subtract, multiply, divide, square or take a square root.
Change an equation into a different form by doing the same thing to both sides, for example until it reads y = ...
The letter on its own on one side of a formula. In y = 3x − 5, y is the subject. 'Make y the subject' means rearrange until it reads y = ...
'Write P in terms of A' means write a formula for P that uses only A and numbers, like P = 4√A.
Introduces a fact you must take as true and use. 'Given that f(2) = 5' means use f(2) = 5 in your working.

Rewrite a quadratic with a squared bracket: x<sup>2</sup> + 6x + 1 = (x + 3)<sup>2</sup> − 8. Half the number in front of x goes in the bracket; then subtract that half squared (here 9). If x<sup>2</sup> has a number in front, take it out first.
x = (−b ± √(b<sup>2</sup> − 4ac)) ÷ (2a) solves any equation ax<sup>2</sup> + bx + c = 0. It is in the formula booklet.
A decreasing function goes down as x goes up: a bigger input gives a smaller output. f(x) = −6x − 3 is decreasing.
A strict inequality uses < or >, so the end value is not included. ≤ and ≥ are not strict: the end value is included.
Allow only some inputs, for example only x ≥ 1. This is often done so that a function becomes one-to-one and has an inverse.
A formula or function that describes a real situation, like C(n) = 5n for the cost of n items at $5 each.
Speed in a given direction, for example 5 metres per second to the right.
The total distance around the edge of a shape. A square with side x has perimeter 4x.
The opposite of a power, coming later in Topic 2: log<sub>10</sub> 100 = 2 because 10<sup>2</sup> = 100. Not needed today.
The digits of a number counted from the first one that is not 0. To 3 significant figures, 3.14159 is 3.14 and 0.004567 is 0.00457.
An exact answer has no rounding: √2 or 1/3, not 1.41 or 0.333.
All the numbers on the number line: whole numbers, negatives, fractions, decimals and numbers like √2 and π. The symbol is ℝ.
The set (collection) of all real numbers. 'x ∈ ℝ' means x can be any number on the number line.
Means 'is in' or 'belongs to'. x ∈ ℝ means x is a real number.
Infinity: not a number, but the idea of going on without end. [1, ∞[ means every number from 1 upwards, with no top end.
'Plus or minus': both signs. y = ±3 means y = 3 or y = −3.
The ring sign for a composite function. (f ∘ g)(x) means f(g(x)), read 'f of g of x': g acts first, then f.
Means 'is sent to'. x ↦ x + 1 is the rule that sends each input x to x + 1.
'Is not equal to'. x ≠ 5 means x can be any number except 5.
The symbols used to write maths. In function notation, f(x) means 'the output of f when the input is x'.
The real situation a question is about, such as a ball being thrown or the cost of items in a shop.
Graphic display calculator: the graphing calculator allowed in Paper 2, for example the TI-84 Plus CE or the Casio fx-CG50.
The part of a graph the GDC screen shows, set by the smallest and largest x-values and y-values. A small window can hide a feature.
Drawn with equal, measured steps along the axes, so positions on the paper match the numbers exactly.
The answer to an addition is a sum, to a subtraction a difference, to a multiplication a product. For 7 and 3: the sum is 10, the difference is 7 − 3 = 4, the product is 21.
Standard Level, the IB maths course you take. 'SL 2.2' is the official number of a topic in the IB syllabus (the list of what the course covers).
Higher Level, the longer IB maths course. HL-only content is not on your SL exam.
Additional Higher Level: the topics only HL students study. 'AHL 2.14' is an HL-only topic, not on your exam.
The IB word at the start of a question, like 'find', 'state' or 'sketch'. It tells you exactly what kind of answer gets the marks.
IB command term: work out the answer and show the main steps of your working.
IB command term: give the answer with little or no calculation. You do not need to show working.
IB command term: use the answer you have just found to get the next result. 'Hence or otherwise' also allows a different method.
IB command term: give the steps of a calculation that lead to the result. In 'show that' the answer is given, so the marks are for the working.
IB command term: give a short answer (a name, a value or a fact) without explanation or calculation.
IB command term: draw the general shape with its key points labelled (intercepts, turning points, asymptotes). It does not need to be to scale.
IB command term: an accurate, labelled graph in pencil, to scale, with points plotted correctly and a ruler for straight lines.
IB command term: find the value or values that make an equation true, using algebra, a graph or the GDC.
The function that changes nothing: it sends every x to x itself, written x ↦ x. A function followed by its inverse is the identity: f(f<sup>−1</sup>(x)) = x.
IB command term: give a full answer that includes the reasons why, not just the result.
IB command term: work out the one correct answer. In everyday words: find.
A function is not defined at a value when it gives no output there, for example 3/(x − 2) at x = 2, because you cannot divide by 0.
Gets closer and closer to. 'As x gets very large, 1/x tends to 0' means 1/x gets as close to 0 as you like.
A function with the same output for every input, like f(x) = 5. Its graph is a horizontal line.
In maths, a collection of numbers (or other things). 'The set of all outputs' means every output, collected together.

A short way to write all the numbers between two ends. [a, b] includes both ends; ]a, b[ includes neither (the bracket turns away from an end that is left out). So [1, 5] is 1 ≤ x ≤ 5 and ]1, 5[ is 1 < x < 5.
Mark a point on a graph at its exact coordinates, for example the point (2, 5): 2 across, 5 up.
In IB maths, technology means your GDC (or graphing software) used to draw graphs and find values such as zeros and intersections.
Write it in exactly that shape and find the numbers that the letters stand for. x<sup>2</sup> + 12x + 24 in the form (x + h)<sup>2</sup> + k is (x + 6)<sup>2</sup> − 12, so h = 6 and k = −12.
Vertical means straight up and down, like the y-axis or the line x = 2. Horizontal means flat, left to right, like the x-axis or the line y = 1.
The maximum is the largest value a function reaches, the minimum the smallest. The maximum point is where it happens on the graph, like (1, 4); the maximum value is its y-coordinate, 4.
A fraction with x in the bottom, like 1/(x − 2) or (2x + 1)/(x − 3). Its graph has asymptotes. It comes later in the course (SL 2.8).
Moving, stretching or flipping a graph, for example moving y = x<sup>2</sup> up by 3 gives y = x<sup>2</sup> + 3. It comes later in the course (SL 2.11).
A word the Khan Academy page uses: an expression with two parts added or subtracted, like x + 1. (x + 1)(x + 2) is a product of two binomials.
